rv.q: That’s bad news for America, but good news for theatergoers, as “Clybourne Park” proves itself more vital and relevant than ever on a big Broadway stage.
In Pam MacKinnon's expert staging, this is provocative entertainment that generates as much uneasiness as laughter.
'Clybourne Park' is everything you want in a play: Smart, witty, provocative and wonderfully acted.
Bruce Norris's brilliant, bracingly uncomfortable comedy about race and real estate in America has lost none of its sting in the move from off-Broadway to the Theatre.
If the walls in the modest bungalow in this ever-changing Chicago neighborhood could talk, they would be crabby. And why not?
The problem is that Norris has given us types rather than fully rounded characters.
His script is lean and mean and raises smart ideas about great divides between races, classes and sexes.

"Clybourne Park," Bruce Norris' shameless and brilliant satire of race, liberal attitudes, white flight and gentrification in suburbia, ought to have transferred straight to Broadway right after its lauded Off-Broadway premiere...
Thankfully, Pam MacKinnon's crackerjack production hasn't lost any of its punch since its 2010 premiere.
While that’s the interpretation I prefer, there’s nothing awry about the show on Broadway, where it provides all the food for thought and lets you do the grazing by yourself.
The play is without question worth seeing, the reward of doing so the satisfaction not only of crackling theater but of keeping up with what's happening in the culture.
A smartly-written play sure to provoke conversation afterwards, many others are sure to enjoy the nasty conflicts that erupt when presumably nice people show their true colors.
